questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ulceroglandular (skin ulcer with regional adenopathy) (2) Glandular (regional adenopathy without a visible skin lesion) (3) Oculoglandular (painful conjunctivitis with ipsilateral preauricular adenopathy) (4) Pneumonic (pulmonary infection from inhalation or hematogenous spread). [Also pharyngeal and typhoidal.]
b) (1) Bite of an infected arthropod (tick or biting fly) (2) Contact with contaminated animal products/carcasses (also aerosol inhalation, contaminated water/mud).
c) (1) Ticks (Dermacentor variabilis, D. andersoni, Amblyomma americanum) (2) Biting/deer flies (Chrysops); mosquitoes in Scandinavia.
d) (1) Streptomycin or gentamicin (aminoglycoside, drug of choice for severe disease) (2) Ciprofloxacin or doxycycline (mild-moderate/oral).

cohort_answer.text: Clinical manifestations: Glandular; Ulceroglandular; Oculoglandular; Pneumonic; Pharyngeal; Typhoidal. Transmission: Animal contact (direct or indirect) with infected animals; Airborne transmission; Arthropod bites; Contaminated food or water. Animal vectors: Rabbits; Rodents (vole). Antibiotics: Doxycycline; Ciprofloxacin; Gentamicin

questions.question: Tularemia: state four clinical types, two animals that carry it, two modes of acquisition, and two treatments.

parts.text: State four clinical types, two animals that carry it, two modes of acquisition, and two treatments.

parts_raw.text: Tularemia four clinical types, two animal that carry, two modes of acquisition, and two treatments.

questions.model_answer:
Four clinical types: (1) Ulceroglandular – skin ulcer at inoculation site with tender regional adenopathy (2) Glandular – regional adenopathy without a visible skin lesion (3) Oculoglandular – painful conjunctivitis with ipsilateral preauricular adenopathy (4) Pneumonic – pulmonary disease from inhalation or hematogenous spread. (Pharyngeal and typhoidal are the other two of six classic forms.)
Two animal reservoirs: lagomorphs (rabbits/hares) and rodents (voles, muskrats, squirrels, beavers).
Two modes of acquisition: bite of an infected arthropod (tick or biting fly); contact with/handling or ingestion of infected animal tissue (also aerosol inhalation, contaminated water).
Two treatments: aminoglycoside (streptomycin or gentamicin) for severe disease; ciprofloxacin or doxycycline for mild-moderate/oral therapy.

cohort_answer.text: Clinical types: Typhoidal: bacteremic with hypotension; no cutaneous lesions. Oculoglandular: result of splash infected material into conjunctiva associated with preauricular tender lymphadenopathy. Oropharyngeal: resulting of eating contaminated meat or drinking contaminated water. Pneumonic: either due to hematogenous spread or inhalation of infected aerosols or aspiration from infected pharynx. Ulceroglandular: skin lesion due to bite of vector and regional adenopathy. Glandular: tender regional adenopathy without evidence of skin bite. Animals that carry: Rabbits, rodents, bobcats, cats. Vectors: Tick/flies/mosquitoes (mnemonic TOO-PUG). Modes of acquisition: Ingestion/inhalation; Inoculation through skin/bite (arthropod bite, contaminated animal product); Splashes; Aerosols - can be used as bioterrorism. Treatment: Severe/mod disease: Streptomycin 1gm IM/IV q12h x 7-10 days or (Gentamicin or Tobramycin 5mg/kg IV divided q8h x 10 days). If hematogenous meningitis: Aminoglycoside + chloramphenicol 50-100 mg/kg/day IV in 4 divided doses. Alternative: mild - Cipro 400mg IV or 750mg PO bid x14-21 days or Doxy 100mg PO BID x 14-21d. Pregnancy: streptomycin or chloramphenicol 15mg/kg qid at least 14 days. Prophylaxis: for aerosol exposures not for natural exposures: Doxy 100mg po BID x 14 d or cipro 500mg PO BID x 14 day. In situation of outbreak/bioterrorism, would use Doxy/Cipro

parts.text: Name 4 common clinical features (on presentation) of Francisella tularensis infection.
What are two important animal reservoirs of this organism?

What are two antimicrobials that are effective against Francisella tularensis?

parts_raw.text: Name 4 common clinical features (on presentation) of Francisella tularensis infection?
What are two important animal reservoirs of this organism?
What are two modes of transmission from animals to humans?
What are two antimicrobials that are effective against Francisella tularensis?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Abrupt fever with chills, headache and malaise (often with a pulse-temperature deficit) (2) A skin ulcer with tender regional lymphadenopathy (ulceroglandular presentation) (3) Painful conjunctivitis with preauricular adenopathy (oculoglandular) (4) Cough/pleuritic chest pain from pneumonia. [Pharyngeal and typhoidal forms also occur.]
b) (1) Lagomorphs – rabbits and hares (2) Rodents – voles, muskrats, squirrels, beavers.
c) (1) Bite of an infected tick or biting fly (2) Direct contact with infected animal carcasses/products (skinning, dressing, or eating undercooked meat).
d) (1) An aminoglycoside – streptomycin or gentamicin (2) Ciprofloxacin (or doxycycline).

cohort_answer.text: Clinical features: typhoidal/septic (systemic disease without lesions or lymphadenitis), oculoglandular (conjunctivitis and pre-auricular lymphadenopathy), oropharyngeal (painful ulcerations from ingesting infected meat/water), pneumonic (inhaled organisms), ulceroglandular (bites/scratches/handling carcasses), glandular (micro-abrasions). Reservoirs: small mammals - voles, mice, water rats, squirrels, rabbits, hares (via tick/fly/mosquito bites and contact with contaminated environments). Transmission: direct contact with infected carcasses or inhalation of contaminated dust, bites/scratches from infected animals, ingestion of undercooked infected meat. Antimicrobials: streptomycin (preferred), IV gentamicin/tobramycin (alternative), x10 days; if meningitis - aminoglycoside + chloramphenicol; bioterrorism setting - doxycycline (14-21d) or ciprofloxacin (14d) PO.

questions.question: Tularemia: list four clinical syndromes (there are actually six).

parts.text: List four clinical syndromes (there are actually six).

parts_raw.text: A) 4 syndromes (there are actually 6)

questions.model_answer: (1) Ulceroglandular – skin ulcer with tender regional adenopathy (2) Glandular – tender regional adenopathy without a visible cutaneous lesion (3) Oculoglandular – painful conjunctivitis with ipsilateral preauricular adenopathy (Parinaud syndrome) (4) Pneumonic – pulmonary disease from inhalation or hematogenous spread. [The remaining two are pharyngeal (exudative pharyngitis/tonsillitis with neck mass) and typhoidal (febrile illness without prominent adenopathy).]

cohort_answer.text: Ulceroglandular tularemia (enlarged tender localized LAD with cutaneous ulcer); Glandular tularemia (enlarged tender localized LAD without cutaneous lesion); Oculoglandular tularemia (including Parinaud's syndrome); Pharyngeal (oropharyngeal) tularemia (severe pharyngitis, neck mass, fever); Pneumonic tularemia (from inhalation or secondary hematogenous spread); Typhoidal tularemia (fever without LAD). Secondary skin manifestations common: erythema nodosum, erythema multiforme, maculopapular (speaker notes: Glandular, oculoglandular, respiratory)

questions.question: Tularemia: list two methods of transmission.

parts.text: List two methods of transmission.

parts_raw.text: B) 2 methods of transmission?

questions.model_answer: (1) Bite of an infected arthropod – most often ticks, also biting/deer flies and mosquitoes (2) Contact with contaminated animal products/carcasses (skinning, dressing, or ingesting undercooked infected meat). Additional routes: inhalation of infectious aerosols (e.g. lawn mowing/brush cutting) and contaminated water or mud. Human-to-human spread does not occur.

cohort_answer.text: Vector borne (mostly ticks, also mosquitos, horse flies, fleas, lice); Animal contact; Foodborne/waterborne; Airborne (lawn mowing or cutting brush); Laboratory (potential for bioterrorism)

questions.question: Tularemia: outline treatment.

parts.text: Outline treatment.

parts_raw.text: D) Treatment

questions.model_answer: Severe disease: an aminoglycoside is the drug of choice – streptomycin 10 mg/kg IM q12h (max 2 g/d) or gentamicin 5 mg/kg/d IM/IV for 7–10 days; streptomycin preferred in adults, gentamicin preferred in children. Mild-to-moderate disease (oral): ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID x10–14 d or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID x14–21 d. Meningitis (rare): aminoglycoside plus ciprofloxacin, doxycycline, or chloramphenicol for 14–21 d. Beta-lactams and macrolides are unreliable. Adjunct: drainage of suppurative nodes.

cohort_answer.text: Moderate to severe: Gentamicin 5mg/kg/day IV divided TID x 7-10 days. Mild: Cipro x14d or Doxy x14d. Meningitis (rare): Gentamicin + Doxy/cipro or chloramphenicol x14-21 days

questions.question: Tularemia: describe prophylaxis (post-exposure).

parts.text: Describe prophylaxis (post-exposure).

parts_raw.text: E) PPX?

questions.model_answer: Prophylaxis after low-risk exposures (e.g. a tick bite) is NOT recommended – observe for fever/illness. For adults with suspected or proven high-risk exposure: ciprofloxacin 500 mg PO BID or doxycycline 100 mg PO BID for 14 days. After a bioterrorism/aerosol exposure, all exposed persons (any age) should receive oral doxycycline or ciprofloxacin for 14 days (a fluoroquinolone may be preferred as it remains effective if delayed). Exposed children are observed without antibiotics except in a bioterrorism event. No prophylaxis is needed for contact with a tularemia patient, as human-to-human spread does not occur. There is no licensed vaccine available.

cohort_answer.text: Avoid exposure (no vaccine). Abx ppx after potential exposures of unknown risk not recommended - watchful waiting. Adults with suspected/proven high risk exposure: Cipro 500mg BID or Doxy 100mg BID x14d. Children: exposures other than bioterrorism event should be observed without prophylactic antibiotics; PEP in children indicated following exposure to F. tularensis bioweapon - Ciprofloxacin 15mg/kg PO BID or Doxycycline 2.2mg/kg PO BID x14 days

parts.text: Give a differential diagnosis.

parts_raw.text: F) DDX:

questions.model_answer: By syndrome: Ulceroglandular/glandular – pyogenic bacterial infection, cat-scratch disease, syphilis, chancroid, lymphogranuloma venereum, tuberculosis, nontuberculous mycobacteria, toxoplasmosis, sporotrichosis, rat-bite fever, anthrax, plague, HSV. Oculoglandular – pyogenic bacterial, adenoviral, syphilis, cat-scratch disease, HSV. Pharyngeal – streptococcal pharyngitis, infectious mononucleosis, adenovirus, diphtheria, tuberculosis. Pneumonic – Mycoplasma, Legionella, Chlamydia pneumoniae, Q fever, psittacosis, tuberculosis, endemic mycoses. Typhoidal – typhoid fever, brucellosis, Legionella, Q fever, disseminated mycobacterial/fungal infection, rickettsioses, malaria, endocarditis.

cohort_answer.text: Mycoplasma pneumoniae; Legionella infection; Chlamydia pneumoniae infection; Q fever; Psittacosis; TB; Endemic mycoses; Yersinia pestis. Additional ddx by syndrome given: ulceroglandular/glandular (pyogenic bacterial, cat-scratch, syphilis, chancroid, LGV, TB, NTM, toxoplasmosis, sporotrichosis, rat-bite fever, anthrax, plague, HSV); oculoglandular (pyogenic bacterial, adenoviral, syphilis, cat-scratch, HSV); pharyngeal (streptococcal pharyngitis, mono, adenoviral, diphtheria, TB); typhoidal (typhoid fever, brucellosis, Legionella, Q fever, disseminated mycobacterial/fungal, rickettsioses, malaria, endocarditis)

questions.question: Tularemia: describe methods of diagnosis.

parts.text: Describe methods of diagnosis.

parts_raw.text: A) Methods of diagnosis?

questions.model_answer: (1) Clinical suspicion – diagnosis ultimately rests on it; notify the laboratory (Tier 1 select agent; handle isolates under BSL-3). (2) Serology – the most common means of confirmation: tube- or micro-agglutination (or ELISA); presumptive titer ≥1:160 (tube) or ≥1:128 (micro), definitive = fourfold rise between acute and convalescent sera (positive after ~2 weeks, peaks 4–5 weeks). (3) Culture – rarely positive and slow; grows poorly on routine/blood agar, needs cysteine-enriched media (chocolate, modified Thayer-Martin, cysteine heart agar) from blood, node, wound, pleural fluid, or sputum. (4) Direct methods – DFA/immunohistochemical staining of smears/tissue, and PCR (e.g. tul4 target) available in Laboratory Response Network labs. (5) MALDI-TOF for isolate identification (note automated systems misidentify it as Haemophilus/Aggregatibacter).

cohort_answer.text: Inform lab (BSL3); MALDI-TOF; cultures rarely positive, does not grow well on routine media - consider chocolate agar or modified Thayer-Martin media; catalase+, gram negative coccobacilli, oxidase-; acute and convalescent serology (4x increase) - most likely means of confirming dx; immunohistochemical staining of smears/tissues; PCR testing (specialized labs)

questions.model_answer:
a) Toxoplasma gondii; specimen: serum; test: Toxoplasma IgG/IgM serology (acute and convalescent). [Beyond this chapter.]
b) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (cervical scrofula); specimen: fine-needle aspirate or excisional lymph node biopsy; test: AFB smear, mycobacterial culture and NAAT. [Beyond this chapter.]
c) Francisella tularensis (ulceroglandular tularemia); specimen: serum (organism rarely seen/grown, and culture is hazardous); test: tube- or micro-agglutination serology, acute and convalescent (fourfold rise); node aspirate can be sent for PCR/culture on cysteine-enriched media at a reference lab under BSL-3.
d) Streptococcus pyogenes; specimen: throat swab; test: rapid antigen and/or throat culture. [Beyond this chapter.]
questions.beyond_mandell: Parts a, b and d (Toxoplasma, TB adenitis, S. pyogenes) are outside the Francisella chapter; answered from standard ID knowledge (Mandell relevant chapters/IDSA).

cohort_answer.text: Steak tartar: Toxoplasma gondii. Blood serology acute and convalescent. Immigrant from Vietnam: Tuberculosis adenitis - fine needle aspiration or excisional biopsy for AFB and mycobacterial culture. Rabbit bite: Francisella tularensis, blood serology at time of presentation and 2-4 weeks after. Inflamed tonsils: Strep pyogenes. Pharyngeal culture. Parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal collection may need to be drained and can be cultured

questions.model_answer: (1) Rickettsial: Rickettsia africae - African tick-bite fever (fever, multiple inoculation eschars, regional lymphadenopathy). (2) Bacterial (non-rickettsial): Francisella tularensis - ulceroglandular tularaemia (cutaneous ulcer/eschar with tender regional lymphadenopathy). (3) Viral: Variola/orthopoxvirus (smallpox or vaccinia) - vesiculopustular lesions crusting into eschars.
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the rickettsial cause is in this chapter (Table 185.3). Bacterial and viral eschar causes are from standard ID sources, not this chapter.

questions.model_answer: a) Leishmania spp. amastigotes (intracellular, 1-5 microns, with nucleus and kinetoplast, within macrophages). b) Nocardia spp. (branching, filamentous, beaded gram-positive rods). c) Francisella tularensis (tiny gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey; oxidase-negative). d) Sporothrix schenckii (small ~1-3 micron cigar-shaped budding yeast; ovoid conidia on conidiophores in mould phase).
questions.beyond_mandell: Only the Sporothrix cigar-shaped yeast morphology is grounded in the slice (p. 3134); the other identifications are standard microbiology.

cohort_answer.text:
Image 1: Leishmania spp. amastigotes, H&E stain - spherical to ovoid, 1-5 µm long by 1-2 µm wide, large nucleus, prominent kinetoplast, short axoneme (rarely visible by light microscopy); reside in macrophages.
Image 2: Nocardia - branching, filamentous, beaded, gram-positive rods with right angle branching (compare/contrast with Rhodococcus equi).
Image 3: Francisella tularensis - tiny, gram-negative coccobacilli, no growth on MacConkey; 'junky' gram stain of tiny GNCB's, DDx Francisella or Brucella; oxidase negative, urease negative, weakly catalase positive, strict aerobes.
Image 4: Sporothrix schenckii - small (~2 microns); PAS stained tissue section showing budding yeast-like cells; conidiophores and conidia are ovoid, elongated, 3-6 x 2-3 µm, one-celled, smooth walled, hyaline.
